title: Dan Ives Thinks AI Buildout Still In Early Stages, With NVDA, MSFT, PLTR, AAPL And CRWD As Top AI Picks - Stocktwits
content: The global shift toward artificial intelligence is still in its infancy, and market investors continue to underestimate the magnitude of an impending multi-trillion-dollar expenditure cycle, tech industry analyst Dan Ives told CNBC. Initiating coverage across nearly 50 technology firms, Ives outlined an extremely optimistic outlook for the sector. Ives emphasized that despite geopolitical tensions, macroeconomic headwinds, and ongoing regulatory debates, the market is misjudging the scale of an incoming $4 trillion spending wave. "We believe this is the 3rd inning of a 9-inning game, and the scale of what is now committed is the evidence," Ives said in an interview with CNBC, noting that secondary and tertiary market opportunities from AI adoption are only beginning to unfold across the corporate landscape. Ives identified chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA) and Microsoft (MSFT) as primary infrastructure beneficiaries. He assigned an "outperform" rating and a $300 price target to Nvidia—implying 25% upside—noting that chip demand is rapidly expanding beyond traditional hyperscalers into sovereign AI initiatives, enterprise networks, and specialized cloud developers. Microsoft received a $615 price target, a 16% gain from Tuesday's closing price. Ives pointed to the firm's expanding commercial remaining performance obligations—which reached $678 billion—as proof of broadening enterprise adoption outside of foundational frontier-model developers. Ives noted that AI systems expand security vulnerabilities faster than existing corporate IT budgets can address. Consequently, cybersecurity expenditures are projected to double, climbing from approximately 5% of overall enterprise IT spending to 10% within the next three years. As frontier labs push deeper into security architecture, cybersecurity companies are entering a prolonged growth cycle. Within this segment, Ives highlighted Palantir Technologies (PLTR) with a $250 price target (30% upside) and CrowdStrike (CRWD) with a $335 price target (20% upside). Beyond mega-cap technology stalwarts and Apple, Ives spotlights smaller, specialized players positioned for significant potential gains. Cloud hardware vendor Boost Run (BRUN) received a $24 price target, representing an estimated 58% upside following strong quarterly results that show it is converting contract backlogs into top-line scale. Additionally, sidewalk robotics firm Serve Robotics (SERV) was given an $8 target (67% upside), with Ives identifying the company as an early frontrunner in autonomous last-mile delivery services. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘neutral’ with ‘normal’ message volumes across all three stocks. NVDA stock has gained 26%, MSFT has risen 9%, and CRWD stock has added 124% year-to-date. The firm increased its rating to ‘Outperform’ from ‘In Line’ and raised its price target to $300 from $210. If traditional seasonality holds, the analyst estimates growth could instead reach the low-20% range in fiscal 2027. Evercore also forecasts earnings per share of about $11, compared with the Wall Street consensus of $10.01. Evercore’s upgrade comes after Goldman Sachs and TD Cowen raised their price target of NTAP stock on Tuesday. Goldman raised its target to $240 from $210 and maintained a ‘Buy’ rating after NetApp’s INSIGHT customer event and investor technology session last week. The firm pointed to new products and expanded capabilities aimed at data infrastructure needs among neoclouds, hyperscalers, enterprises and sovereign customers. The company completed its acquisition of TopBuild in July and expanded product offerings and installation capabilities, adding exposure to markets such as data centers. The deal is expected to produce at least $300 million in annual synergies by 2030, largely from procurement, pricing, and cross-selling. Shares of major farm-equipment makers fell on Wednesday after the Federal Trade Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture opened a broad inquiry into business practices across the agricultural equipment market. At the time of writing, Deere & Co. (DE) was down 3%, AGCO Corp (AGCO) slumped nearly 6%, clocking its worst day since June, while CNH Industrial (CNH) shares declined 5.3%. Shares of Caterpillar (CAT), which manufactures small dozers and loaders for farming, also traded 6% lower. The FTC and USDA are asking farmers, repair shops, dealers and industry employees to share information about possible barriers to buying, servicing and repairing agricultural equipment. The agencies said the inquiry follows a “growing number of complaints” from farmers who say they face barriers to acquiring equipment and the services needed to keep it operating. Regulators are also seeking examples of “restrictions, penalties or retaliation” and information on how industry practices may affect pricing, competition, innovation and farmer welfare. Public comments on the inquiry are open until December 7, the notice read. The latest inquiry comes just months after the FTC reached a settlement with Deere over restrictions on farmers’ ability to repair John Deere equipment. As part of the settlement, Deere must give farmers and independent repair shops access to the same repair tools and software available to its authorized dealers for the next 10 years. The FTC said that settlement will ensure that farmers can “enjoy the right to repair their own John Deere tractors and farm equipment.” Retail sentiment surrounding DE and CNH on Stocktwits turned ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’ over the past 24 hours, while sentiment around AGCO and CAT was ‘bullish.’ One retail trader on the platform said DE stock was “way oversold” DE shares have been on a smashing run this year, surging 196%. On October 8, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI's annualized revenue was about $50 billion, roughly $20 billion below figures widely reported in September. AI stocks sold off. Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) dropped about 3%, erasing roughly $170 billion in value, while Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) fell more than 4%. Just hours later, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI expects to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by year-end. The gap came down to how revenue was counted. The higher figure includes sales through OpenAI's cloud partners, which OpenAI's own number leaves out. Bloomberg's report suggests OpenAI could reach $70 billion in annualized revenue by year-end, although achieving that target would require substantial growth from September's $50 billion run rate. If the market overreacted to OpenAI's revenue figures, the selloff may have created buying opportunities. These AI stocks may deserve a closer look. Nvidia sells to nearly every major AI lab and cloud provider, so one company's revenue figure says little about its overall demand. Jensen Huang said last month that Nvidia expects to double the number of chips it sells in 2027, and management has guided to about 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028. The company also added a record $150 billion to its buyback, a strong sign of confidence in its cash flow. ​The valuation makes the selloff even harder to justify. The forward non-GAAP P/E of 25.50x sits about 40% below its 5-year average of 42.15x. Similarly, the forward Price-to-sales ratio of 13.93x is 29% below its average of 19.67x. So even while sitting at the center of the AI boom, Nvidia's stock trades at a considerable discount. The EPS outlook is solid. Analysts expect earnings to grow 95% this fiscal year and 71% the next. Based on fiscal 2028 earnings, the P/E falls to about 15x.Nvidia held approximately $23.2 billion in net cash, including marketable debt securities, as of July 26, 2026. The stock's valuation may look more attractive than the recent sell-off suggests, but it's not the only stock near record levels that Wall Street is watching. See the 10 best stocks near all-time highs to buy, with NVDA ranked No. 1. Broadcom's link to OpenAI is more direct. It's building OpenAI's custom AI chips under a 10-gigawatt deal. The night before, the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was working to arrange more than $50 billion in financing tied to that work. Talks were described as early, and Bloomberg's account put the debt at about $30 billion for the next phase. Landing a day ahead of the OpenAI revenue headline, the report made the risk look bigger. Even so, the financing is still in early talks, and the $70 billion is a projection, not cash in hand. The chip rollout extends through 2029, meaning OpenAI's growth must continue well beyond this year. Broadcom's forward non-GAAP P/E of 32.30x sits about 18% above its 5-year average of 27.34x. ASML (NASDAQ:ASML) doesn't get as much attention as chip stocks like Nvidia do, but the European semiconductor capital equipment specialist is arguably just as crucial to the AI boom. ASML is the world's only manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment, which is used by manufacturers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Intel, and Samsung to make the world's most advanced chips. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. Continue » The company is downstream from fabless chip companies like Nvidia in the AI boom, but it's set to reap the rewards of surging demand for AI chips, including the memory chip shortage and the supply expansion now underway. With ASML set to report third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, let's review what to expect from the company to determine if the stock is a buy. ASML stock is up 64% this year, benefiting from the larger boom in chip stocks in the spring, though it's traded sideways over the last few months. Investors bid the stock up on expectations that its growth will accelerate due to semiconductor supply shortages, and that seems to be happening. The analyst consensus calls for ASML's revenue to jump 56% to 11.7 billion euros, or $13.1 billion, and for adjusted earnings per share to nearly double from 5.49 euros to 10.76 euros. ASML's quarterly results are lumpy as its machines are very expensive and it sells around 100 of them each quarter. However, it also earns significant revenue from installed base management, which covers maintenance, repair, and upgrades to existing machines. The forecast calls for ASML's strongest revenue growth since 2023, and significantly higher than the 24% growth it reported in the second quarter. The boom in memory explains part of the growth surge as the company has projected more than 75% growth in memory systems for the year, due to ramping demand for high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, and top customers like TSMC and Intel are expanding production of more advanced nodes. With the stock having roughly doubled over the last year, ASML can't be considered cheap anymore. It currently trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 57, which is higher than many of its chip-stock peers, such as Nvidia, as well as ETFs that track the industry, such as the Van Eck Semiconductor ETF. However, ASML is a rare monopoly, as the only maker of EUV machines, that investors have access to, and its market power grows as demand for more advanced chips leads manufacturers to buy more EUV machines. The company also has a less advanced deep ultraviolet (DUV) machine, with which it competes with Chinese companies and others such as Nikon and Canon. While others are developing EUV technology, the company's lead in the industry seems reasonably secure due to its experience, specialized supply chain, technical expertise, and relationships. Finally, investors will want to watch ASML's guidance in the report. The company has issued 2030 revenue guidance of 44 billion-60 billion euros, but analysts' expectations for the third quarter show it's already reached that rate, meaning it could soon raise its long-term guidance. The company has already raised its 2026 guidance to 43 billion-45 billion euros from an earlier forecast of 36 billion-40 billion euros. Based on the momentum in the business, the monopoly in EUVs, and the growth in chip demand from AI, ASML looks like a strong buy ahead of its report. Though its quarterly results are difficult to predict, the company should achieve considerable growth over the next few years. title: NVDA Stock Falls to $225 as Microsoft Chip and Talks to Invest in Reflection AI Raise Debt Fears - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia shares have retreated from a record above $243 toward $225 as Microsoft’s new Maia 300 chip, questions about OpenAI’s underlying revenue and growing debt requirements for data-center expansion raise concerns about the sustainability of semiconductor demand. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares have fallen from their record above $243 toward $225, giving back part of their recent rally and moving closer to the $6 trillion valuation milestone before the reversal. The latest decline reflects renewed selling across semiconductor stocks and questions about whether infrastructure spending can justify elevated valuations. Shares fell more than 1% in the latest session as Microsoft introduced its third-generation Maia 300 processor, designed to improve efficiency and reduce the cost of running workloads across its cloud and software businesses. Microsoft’s Maia 300 reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Its 96-accelerator configuration is also designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of its predecessor, Maia 200. The development highlights Microsoft’s efforts to improve computing efficiency and potentially reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. Although Nvidia remains central to the semiconductor ecosystem, growing in-house chip development could introduce longer-term competitive pressure. Nvidia is reportedly considering acquiring Reflection AI or increasing its existing investment in the startup, which develops open-weight models and software-development tools. Nvidia has already invested $800 million, according to reports, but discussions remain preliminary and no agreement has been reached. A potential transaction could deepen Nvidia’s exposure to software and model development, although it would also add another investment commitment. Concerns have also emerged after OpenAI’s annualised revenue run rate was reported at approximately $50 billion at the end of September, below the widely circulated $68 billion figure. The higher number reportedly included revenue generated by partners. Despite strong reported growth, the distinction has raised questions about the financial assumptions underpinning the infrastructure buildout. Nvidia, Oracle and CoreWeave could face pressure if investors reassess expected returns from increasingly expensive computing projects. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw a below $230 again. Reports of a potential $40 billion SpaceX financing package for Nvidia GPUs and Amazon’s exploration of an approximately $8 billion chip-financing structure highlight the industry’s capital requirements. Nvidia’s long-term demand outlook remains supported by expanding computing needs, but competition from custom chips and reliance on debt-financed infrastructure are becoming harder to ignore. A sustained recovery will require renewed buying momentum and confidence that customers can turn substantial capital expenditure into durable revenue growth.

title: MSFT, ORCL, NVDA, QQQ In Focus: OpenAI’s Annualized Revenue Reportedly Trails Prior Expectations By $20B - Stocktwits
content: OpenAI’s annualized revenue is about $20 billion lower than previously indicated, financial documents provided to investors reveal, potentially cooling exuberance around the pace of artificial intelligence demand, according to a Financial Times report. In recent communications with investors, the artificial intelligence research and deployment company said its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September. The figure falls well short of the $70 billion estimate widely reported late last month based on data initially supplied to investors, the Financial Times reported. Annualized revenue serves as a primary metric for gauging market adoption across the generative AI sector. Financial analysts closely track the benchmark for both OpenAI and key competitor Anthropic to justify surging public equity valuations and sprawling tech infrastructure expenditures. Most AI-linked stocks, including Microsoft (MSFT), a key OpenAI investor, Oracle (ORCL), Nvidia (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), Intel (INTC), CoreWeave (CRWV), and Cerebras (CBRS), eased on the lower-than-expected annualized revenue. The iShares semiconductor ETF (SOXX) and the VanEck semiconductor ETF (SMH) eased between 2% and 3% on Thursday. OpenAI investors sought to standardize revenue performance against Anthropic, a person familiar with the matter told the Financial Times. The two AI developers use different accounting methods to calculate annualized performance. Anthropic includes revenue generated from cloud platform distribution partners, including Amazon Web Services (AWS) (AMZN) and Google Cloud (GOOG, GOOGL). Conversely, OpenAI excludes sales made through third-party cloud channels from its core calculations. Attempts to "gross up" OpenAI's figures to match Anthropic's reporting structure led to initial estimates that OpenAI had reached $40 billion in annualized revenue in August, according to the Financial Times. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits related to OpenAI was ‘neutral’ with ‘normal’ message volumes. One user highlighted the effect of the lower annualized revenue on the wider tech space. Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) shares drew significant investor attention on Thursday after Starbucks reportedly explored a potential takeover of the restaurant chain. The Financial Times reported that a purchase of Chipotle, with a market value of nearly $41 billion, would be the largest tie-up in the restaurant sector in history. CMG shares were up about 6% at the time of writing on Thursday, while SBUX shares were down about 3%. According to the report, Starbucks has worked with advisers in recent months on a potential takeover proposal for Chipotle. The status of the plans, including whether Starbucks has submitted a formal offer, remains unclear. People familiar with the matter told FT that a transaction of this size may not ultimately move forward. If completed, the transaction would surpass Burger King's $11.4 billion acquisition of Tim Hortons in 2014, making it the largest restaurant acquisition on record, according to FT. The potential combination would bring together two large U.S.-focused restaurant businesses. Starbucks operates about 41,000 owned and licensed stores globally, with roughly two-fifths located in the U.S., while Chipotle has about 4,200 restaurants, almost all in the U.S. Together, the companies generated nearly $50 billion in sales last year, based on their respective reported figures. The potential transaction would also involve Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle for more than six years. Niccol left Chipotle in August 2024 to become Starbucks' chief executive. At Starbucks, Niccol has been overseeing the company's 'Back to Starbucks' strategy, which includes adding baristas, introducing new menu items, speeding up service and renovating cafes. Starbucks has also hired former Chipotle executives Tressie Lieberman and Stephen Piacentini to lead marketing and coffee shop development, respectively, according to the FT. Chipotle recently appointed Sabir Sami, the former CEO of KFC, to its board, effective immediately. The company said Sami brings more than 30 years of global consumer and restaurant-industry experience, including 16 years at Yum! Brands. Separately, Chipotle is expanding its restaurant leadership pipeline as it works toward a long-term goal of 7,000 restaurants across the U.S. and Canada. The company expects to open 350 to 370 new restaurants in 2026 and aims to have an Apprentice in every restaurant by the end of 2027. More than 85% of Chipotle's restaurant managers began their careers as Crew Members, the company said. Shares of Immunovant (IMVT) sold off Thursday as traders treated Argenx’s (ARGX) failed late-stage Sjögren’s trial as a warning for its own experimental drug for the autoimmune disorder. Immunovant (IMVT) fell about 6% to $30.06 in morning trading. Its parent Roivant (ROIV) was also weaker, trading down roughly 2%. Immunovant is developing IMVT-1402 in an ongoing mid-stage study in Sjögren’s disease. Argenx’s efgartigimod works the same way: it lowers circulating IgG antibodies that can drive autoimmune disease. A late-stage failure for a closely related drug raises the odds that simply reducing IgG may not be enough in Sjögren’s. The move also follows Immunovant’s late-September setback, when IMVT-1402 missed its main goal in a cutaneous lupus study, and that program was dropped. Roivant is the majority owner of Immunovant, and IMVT-1402 is central to the group’s autoimmune story. Argenx has stopped its late-stage UNITY study of weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod in adults with moderate-to-severe Sjögren’s disease. An independent monitoring committee, after an interim look, said the trial was unlikely to meet its main goal: a reduction in systemic disease activity at week 48, the company said. Safety matched the drug’s known profile, with no new signals. Sjögren’s, which causes dry eyes, dry mouth, fatigue and joint pain, still has no approved targeted therapy and is unusually varied from patient to patient, which makes trials hard to win. Argenx’s U.S. shares were down about 14% to $797.69. The drug is already approved as Vyvgart for the treatment of generalized myasthenia gravis and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP). The failed trial removes the Sjögren’s path for Vyvgart. H.C. Wainwright analyst Douglas Tsao called it a good-news, bad-news day for Argenx. On the positive side, the analyst said a 126-patient mid-stage study of FB102 in celiac disease met its primary endpoint. Argenx acquired FB102 through its $2.2 billion acquisition of Forte Biosciences. The firm sees that result as real validation of Argenx’s Forte deal and a clear step toward a late-stage study. The UNITY stop, by contrast, was a “surprising setback,” the firm said. Wainwright said it is now more cautious about what the failure implies for Immunovant’s mid-stage Sjögren’s study of IMVT-1402. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is posting the kind of numbers that once justified a sky-high price tag. Yet the market now pays far less for each dollar of its expected profit than it did, on average, over the past five years. Something has to give. Either the earnings engine is about to stall, or the stock's discount is out of date. For anyone who hasn't followed the story, Nvidia designs the chips and systems that train and run artificial intelligence models. Its graphics processors started out in gaming PCs, but today the money comes overwhelmingly from data centers run by cloud giants, AI labs, and governments. It increasingly sells entire racks of processors, networking gear, and software rather than individual chips. Which is it? For investors weighing companies featured among 10 Best Return on Equity (ROE) Stocks to Buy, the answer depends less on Nvidia's record results than on whether its biggest customers can keep paying for them. Nvidia's edge is the whole stack. Developers have spent years building on its CUDA software platform, and moving to a rival means rewriting code and re-tuning systems. That switching cost keeps buyers loyal even as competitors improve. The numbers back it up. In fiscal Q2 2027 (ended in late July), Data Center revenue hit $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year earlier. GAAP gross margin reached 75.0%, compared with 72.4% in the year-ago quarter. A company losing its grip on customers usually has to cut prices; Nvidia's margins went the other way, reflecting the formidable pricing power and balance sheet strength showcased among 10 Stocks With Low Debt and Strong Free Cash Flow. The newest proof is the Vera Rubin platform, which Nvidia says is now in full production. Rubin racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. Total revenue reached $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2, up 106% year over year and 18% from the prior quarter. Management guided fiscal Q3 revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. That outlook assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China, so any reopening there would be extra. Nvidia is also pushing into new territory, with its Vera CPU built for AI agents and the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator (a chip for running models rather than training them) in full production. The moat looks wider, not narrower. Here's the catch. According to CNBC, Nvidia, Oracle, CoreWeave, and other AI stocks fell recently after a report on OpenAI's revenue. That reaction gets at the core worry: a small group of buyers is spending enormous sums well ahead of the revenue AI might eventually generate. Nvidia is even helping finance the buildout. It has set up compute financing platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, aiming to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital, subject to definitive agreements. Bulls see that as clearing a bottleneck. Skeptics see a supplier propping up its own demand, a question that hangs even more heavily over specialized AI cloud providers. For now, navigating this deployment payoff remains the main risk to watch across the 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now. At a forward P/E of 24.62, as of October 9, investors are paying roughly $25 for every $1 of expected earnings. That's well below Nvidia's 5-year average of 42.13 and only a whisker above the sector's 23.35. Now set that against growth. Adjusted EPS (which excludes items Nvidia treats as outside day-to-day operations) came in at $2.22 in fiscal Q2, up from $1.01 a year earlier. GAAP EPS was higher at $2.46, but the adjusted figure gives the cleaner read on the core business. Looking further out, expected EPS growth stands at 70.90% in 2028. A company growing that quickly would normally command a premium to its sector, not near-parity. The market is effectively pricing in a sharp slowdown, which ties straight back to the customer-spending worry. That near-sector multiple also invites comparison with the foundry that manufactures its chips, highlighting why it remains closely watched alongside the other 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy Before They Explode. Professional money hasn't been scared off. Hedge fund interest ticked up, with 285 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 275 in the prior one. Short interest sits at just 1.27% of the float, a sign of relatively limited bearish positioning. The evidence points to a business whose moat is widening while its valuation assumes the opposite. If Rubin keeps ramping and fiscal Q3 lands within its own outlook range, a multiple near the sector's looks hard to defend for long. That setup suits investors with a multiyear horizon who can stomach sharp swings tied to AI spending headlines. What would change the picture is clear: a pullback in spending by the big AI labs and cloud providers, or gross margin slipping meaningfully below the roughly 74% Nvidia has guided for. While we acknowledge the risk and potential of NVDA as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA, XETRA:NVD) shares fell 1% to $226.55, down $2.73, after Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) unveiled a new artificial intelligence chip that threatens to reduce its reliance on the graphics processor maker. Microsoft, the software and cloud computing giant, introduced its third-generation Maia 300 processor on Monday, targeting lower costs and greater efficiency in running AI workloads across its products and services. The chip is designed to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading graphics processing unit (GPU) systems, with a configuration of 96 accelerators offering up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of its predecessor, Maia 200. Microsoft plans to begin deploying Maia 300 in production workloads in 2027 and scale its in-house chip programme to multi-gigawatt deployments, making Maia its primary system for AI inference, the process of running trained models to generate responses. The move presents a potential competitive challenge for Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, whose processors have supplied much of the hardware used to run AI services, as cloud providers seek greater control over infrastructure costs and performance. Microsoft already uses Maia 200 in production, including for Microsoft Copilot, and plans to extend its deployment across additional services as it develops its own AI models and infrastructure. The Maia 300 uses a chiplet architecture built around Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's advanced manufacturing technology, separating computing, memory control and input-output functions to improve efficiency. Nvidia's broader market position will depend on whether demand for AI computing continues to expand enough to offset customers developing their own alternatives, while Microsoft's planned rollout remains more than a year away. title: Nvidia and Micron Technology Just Received Some Very Bad News From an Unlikely Place - The Motley Fool
content: Australian investors just rejected one of the country's biggest artificial intelligence companies. Australia is a relatively small country by population, with just 28 million citizens. But it has become a major hub for artificial intelligence (AI) data center projects because of its vast land mass and favorable political climate. In fact, an Australian company called Firmus built a data center in Melbourne that houses the largest cluster of Nvidia's (NVDA -1.29%) Blackwell Ultra chips in the entire Southern Hemisphere. Last week, Firmus was on track for one of the biggest initial public offerings (IPOs) in the history of the Australian stock market, which would've raised approximately $5 billion (U.S. dollars) at a $30 billion valuation. The company was going to use the funds to build more data centers across Australasia in order to expand its customer base, which already includes OpenAI and Meta Platforms. However, Firmus pulled the plug on its IPO at the last minute due to a lack of investor demand, which suggests funding might be starting to dry up for the AI industry. Mounting losses at some of the world's largest AI labs are an increasing concern, and rising interest rates are giving many investors a risk-free alternative for their money. Here's why this development could have negative consequences for semiconductor suppliers like Nvidia and Micron Technology (MU -3.88%). According to Nvidia, the top-five hyperscale companies (including Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet) are on track to spend around $800 billion on AI data center infrastructure in 2026 and could spend a further $1.3 trillion in 2027. As a result, demand currently outstrips supply for critical chips like the graphics processing units (GPUs) supplied by Nvidia and the accompanying high-bandwidth memory (HBM) supplied by Micron. Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet build this infrastructure to develop their own AI software, but they also rent computing capacity to other businesses via their respective cloud platforms. This practice has become very lucrative, and Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, and Alphabet's Google Cloud each delivered accelerating revenue growth in the quarter ended June 30. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » In theory, hyperscalers will continue building more infrastructure as long as they believe there is demand for computing capacity. But cracks are starting to form; to keep up with the soaring costs of chips and components, companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and even Microsoft have dramatically raised prices for using their AI models and software over the last few months. OpenAI, for instance, recently introduced a new $500-per-month subscription plan for uncapped use of its flagship models, representing a whopping 150% increase over its $200-per-month plan, which used to be its most expensive offering. A report by the Financial Times last Thursday suggests OpenAI's annualized revenue is now tracking at $50 billion, below the $70 billion previously reported by other outlets. That might be a sign customers are pulling back amid the price hikes. That isn't surprising, considering companies like Uber Technologies, Walmart, AT&T, and even Amazon have placed AI usage restrictions on their employees this year to prevent budget blowouts. In fact, a recent survey by UBS Group found that 60% of businesses are diverting some AI workloads to cheaper, more efficient models to reduce costs. These models typically consume less computing power than those from labs like OpenAI, which could result in lower demand for chips. Therefore, Firmus' withdrawn IPO is just one more sign that sentiment toward AI might be shifting, at least temporarily. Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 29.1 as I write this (Oct. 9), which is less than half its 10-year average of 61.3. Micron stock is even cheaper. Its P/E ratio is just 13.9, a sizable discount to both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, which have P/E ratios of 23.3 and 34.6, respectively. With an uncertain demand outlook and more supply scheduled to come online over the next couple of years, it appears Wall Street is betting the data center memory boom will be short lived. So, what should investors do? Those who already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to hold on and take a wait-and-see approach. Over the next month, the hyperscalers will release their operating results for the quarter ended Sept. 30. If they announce a pullback in capital expenditures, a slowdown in semiconductor demand is almost certainly on the horizon, which might be a sign for investors to trim their positions. Investors who don't already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to wait on the sidelines. While they seem cheap at face value, the market is sending a clear message that perhaps these companies won't grow their earnings as fast as initially expected over the next couple of years. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA, XETRA:NVD), the American chipmaker, is reportedly considering an acquisition of Reflection AI or a further investment in the startup as it expands its involvement in open-weight artificial intelligence models. The discussions remain at an early stage, with no terms agreed upon, and could still fall apart, although an agreement could emerge within weeks, Reuters reported, citing the Financial Times. Options under consideration include a full acquisition, an acqui-hire arrangement under which Nvidia would hire Reflection's employees and license its technology, or an agreement to supply additional chips or increase its existing equity stake. Nvidia has already invested $800 million in Reflection, a company founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou. Laskin, Reflection's chief executive, was seeking new investment at a valuation of $25 billion before additional funding in April, indicating the possible scale of a transaction. The startup develops artificial intelligence tools for software development and is targeting enterprise customers and governments seeking to build customised AI systems. Reflection launched Beam, its first open-weight AI model, on 5 October, aiming to compete with Chinese models in coding, advanced reasoning and agentic tasks, which involve AI systems carrying out multistep activities. Open-weight models make their trained parameters available to external developers, allowing them to adapt and deploy the technology rather than relying entirely on closed systems controlled by model providers. Reflection says Beam performs comparably to Z.AI's GLM-5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks, positioning the company to challenge lower-cost Chinese alternatives. A transaction would reinforce Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's support for open-weight models and extend the chipmaker's investment in the artificial intelligence ecosystem, where demand for computing power remains central to model development and deployment. Nvidia and Reflection did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the reported discussions, Reuters reported. If it hadn't done that, Nvidia's stock would be valued at over $2,000 per share. When Nvidia split its stock back then, it was worth over $1,000 per share, and I think that will be when the next stock split occurs. There are several factors contributing to this, notably the fact that it's part of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES: ^DJI) (which is weighted based on stock price versus market cap). There are a few stocks in the $800 or higher range that haven't split, but $1,000 is usually the point at which many companies start to consider a split. For Nvidia to reach $1,000 per share, it would have to quadruple. Considering that Nvidia is already a $5.6 trillion company, that would be a huge rise. In fact, for Nvidia to get to $1,000 per share, it would need a market cap of over $24 trillion. That's a long way off, and may cause investors to think that another stock split won't be coming, maybe ever. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » However, some projections suggest Nvidia could reach that level, maybe not in the not-too-distant future, like 2030. So, how will Nvidia get there? Let's do the math and find out. First, let's establish some parameters to assess Nvidia's ending valuation. Right now, Nvidia trades for about 29 times earnings, which is down quite a ways from where it traded at this time last year. The average S&P 500 company trades at about 25.6 times earnings, so a price tag of 30 times earnings is probably pretty cheap. Still, it bakes some conservatism into the estimate. If it's something like 35 times earnings, Nvidia requires a lot less growth to get there. If we take the average of the two and settle at 32.5 times trailing earnings, it would require Nvidia to produce $745 billion in earnings to obtain a $24.2 trillion valuation. Over the past 12 months, Nvidia's profit margin has reached 64%, which is slightly influenced by investment gains. Nvidia's non-GAAP profit margin excludes this, and in Q2 it was 56%. If we use a 55% profit margin, that would require $1.35 trillion in annual revenue. Nvidia may not be as far from hitting that figure as one might think. This year, Wall Street analysts estimate Nvidia will generate $412 billion in revenue. Next year, that figure rises to $692 billion. So, by the end of 2027, it will be over halfway there. With Nvidia's revenue only needing to double in the time frame from 2028 to 2030, this projection just got a bit more palatable. Nvidia has told investors that it expects global annual data center capital expenditures to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion annually by 2030. With the big five artificial intelligence hyperscalers expected to spend about $1.3 trillion next year, that leaves plenty of room for the marketplace to double between 2028 and 2030. So, can Nvidia hit $1,000 per share? I think so, and it may happen as soon as 2030. It won't be an easy path to get there, and there may be bumps along the way, but if any stock can achieve it, I think it's Nvidia. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. A while ago, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) reported a quarter in which revenue more than doubled. Yet the stock's valuation sits far below where it has spent the past five years. That's an odd pairing, and it's the reason the shares deserve a second look. Nvidia designs the processors and networking gear that fill the data centers where AI models are trained and run. Its customers include cloud providers, AI labs, and governments, and most of its sales come from that data center business. So is the lower multiple a bargain, or a hint that the best margins are already in the numbers? The answer depends on whether a new product cycle can sustain profitability. Nvidia's edge isn't a single chip. It sells whole systems: CPUs, GPUs, and the networking that ties thousands of them together. In fiscal Q2 2027, Data Center revenue reached $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year earlier. Gross margin held at 75.0% on both a GAAP and non-GAAP basis, up about 2.5 percentage points year over year on the non-GAAP measure. That pairing is the proof. Buyers with real alternatives push on price, yet Nvidia kept more of each sales dollar while selling far more of them. CEO Jensen Huang said demand is still accelerating, with several frontier AI labs now building in parallel rather than one lab driving the buildout, as was the case a year ago. A rival chipmaker is chasing the same data center dollars from a different angle. See which one. Management guided fiscal Q3 revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, up from the $96.2 billion just reported. Vera Rubin, the next-generation platform, is in full production, with racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. Major cloud buyers moving to the new generation is what suggests the moat is widening rather than merely holding. Nvidia is also helping customers pay for the buildout. It announced partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR on financing platforms meant to mobilize over $500 billion of outside capital, subject to definitive agreements. Shareholders got attention, too. Nvidia returned about $26.0 billion through buybacks and dividends in the quarter, backed by a massive remaining share repurchase authorization of nearly $99 billion. Here's the strongest pushback. Nvidia guided fiscal Q3 gross margin to 74.0%, plus or minus 50 basis points, a modest step down from the 75.0% it just delivered. The outlook also assumes no data center compute revenue from China. Durability is the deeper worry. If AI spending pauses, or inflation and geopolitical concerns keep weighing on the market, growth could cool just as the new platform ramps. That risk is real, but so far it's narrow. The guide still points to higher revenue, and any China sales would land on top of the outlook rather than inside it. Margin is still the number to watch. Looking beyond the chip designers? Here's a list of AI stocks to buy before they explode. On forward earnings, Nvidia trades at 25.67 times, meaning investors pay about $25.67 for every $1 of expected earnings. The sector's multiple is 23.77, and Nvidia's own five-year average is 42.20. So the stock sits only slightly above its peers and well under what the market paid for it through much of the AI boom. Growth is what makes that gap interesting. Analysts expect earnings per share to grow 69.66% in 2027, a pace that, if it arrives, would pull the multiple on today's price down quickly. This analysis leans on non-GAAP earnings. GAAP EPS of $2.46 in fiscal Q2 topped the non-GAAP $2.22 because it included gains on equity securities, which management excludes from the adjusted figure. Since the start of fiscal 2027, Nvidia's non-GAAP results also count stock-based compensation, making that measure a tougher yardstick than before. The catch is that the growth forecast leans on margins and supply holding up. If either slips, a modest multiple would be resting on shakier earnings. Sentiment supports the setup. Hedge fund interest ticked up, with 285 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 275 in the prior one. Short interest is 1.27% of the float, which points to relatively limited bearish positioning. The evidence points to a discount that looks genuine rather than a warning sign. At 25.67 times expected earnings, against a five-year average of 42.20, investors are paying far less for a business that more than doubled revenue and still guided higher. That setup suits investors who can live with swings in AI spending and care more about earnings growth than a smooth ride. A gross margin that falls below the guided 74.0% range, or a quarter where revenue lands under the low end of the $108.0 billion guide, would change the picture. Either would suggest the earnings behind the multiple are softer than hoped. While we acknowledge the risk and potential of NVDA as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame.
